title: The method: transaction by transaction
excerpt: How we turn thousands of transactions scattered across exchanges, wallets and DeFi protocols into a single, traceable tax report, with judgement applied by hand and every figure backed up.

hero.h1: An automated report is the starting point, never the deliverable
hero.subheading: Software processes. Judgement decides. Our method is to rebuild your activity from the raw data and review by hand everything a program can't resolve on its own.

toc.label: What goes wrong in the data

sections.h2: Why running your CSVs through a program isn't enough
sections.body:
Crypto tax tools do one thing well: read lots of files quickly. What they don't do is decide. And in a real portfolio, most of the work is decisions: whether a transfer is a sale or a move between your own wallets, whether a token that turned up at your address is a taxable airdrop or spam, what acquisition value to give something you received without buying it, or what to do with the transactions from an exchange that has shut down and no longer lets you download anything.

A program resolves those situations by applying a default value. Almost always the safest one for the software, which is not the most accurate one for you: zero acquisition cost, transfers treated as disposals, tokens with no market price valued at whatever the first available oracle says. The report comes out, it adds up internally, and it's wrong.

The problem surfaces when that report reaches the Spanish Tax Agency (AEAT). From that point on it's your tax return, and correcting it is harder than getting it right in the first place.

cita.pie: A program resolves grey areas by applying a default value. Almost always the safest one for the software, which is not the most accurate one for you.

sections.h2: What usually goes wrong in the data
bullets: Internal transfers counted as sales: you send funds from your exchange to your cold wallet and the report records it as a disposal. It's the most common error, and the one that creates the most phantom gains.

Token spam: addresses that receive hundreds of worthless tokens sent by third parties. On chains such as Solana or BSC this can mean thousands of records that pollute the whole portfolio if they're processed as income.
Unidentified exchanges of assets (swaps): swapping one token for another is taxable even if it never goes through euros. Many transaction histories don't distinguish a swap from a simple transfer.
Lost acquisition cost: tokens received through staking, airdrops, forks or liquidity rewards that the program values at zero, inflating the gain when you sell them.
Duplicates across sources: the same transaction appears in the exchange's CSV and in the on-chain reading of the wallet.
Defunct exchanges: platforms that have shut down, leaving no downloadable history, whose part of the record has to be rebuilt by other means.
Dates and time zones: records timestamped in different time zones that throw the order of transactions out of sequence and, with it, the FIFO calculation.
sections.entrada: These are the seven failures that come up again and again, and no program resolves any of them on its own.

items: Counts a transfer to your own cold wallet as a sale
Values tokens you received without buying them at zero cost
Processes token spam as if it were income
Applies the price from the first available oracle, without cross-checking
Treats periods with no data as if they never existed
Identifies who owns the destination address and marks the transfer as internal
Rebuilds the acquisition value as at the date of receipt
Filters spam with judgement, not with an automatic list
Cross-checks the price across sources and documents which one was applied
Sets the period aside, rebuilds it indirectly and records the degree of certainty

sections.entrada: Each phase matches one of the four pieces of the symbol, and not by chance: the symbol describes this process.

formas.body: The raw data, exactly as it arrives from the exchange. We check its integrity and spot what's missing before processing anything.
The process that bends the data until it fits: formats, time zones, duplicates and internal transfers.
The judgement. Each transaction is given its tax treatment, and anything that doesn't fit a rule is set aside for manual review.
The result, now closed into the report: the FIFO rule applied to the reconciled portfolio, with the detail behind every total.

sections.body:
We don't review all hundred thousand transactions by hand: we review the ones the automated process can't resolve with certainty, and those are always the ones that decide the result.

The following are set aside for manual review: transfers with no identified counterparty, tokens with no reliable market price on the date of the transaction, acquisitions with no known cost, transactions in DeFi protocols whose mechanics don't fit a standard category, and any period where the data from two sources contradict each other.

In a portfolio of fifty thousand transactions, that list usually runs to between three hundred and two thousand. That's where the risk is concentrated, and it's the work an automated report skips.

bullets: Tax report with the summary and its detail: the totals that go into your tax return and, behind each one, the transactions that make it up.
Criteria memo: which treatment was applied in each grey area and why. It's the document that supports your position if you're ever asked about it.
Issues log: what data was missing, what was rebuilt indirectly and with what degree of certainty.
Reconciled portfolio: the clean dataset, which serves as the starting point for the following tax years without repeating the work.
Supporting documentation: the original files, organised and referenced from the report.

sections.body:
It's also worth saying what the method can't do.

It doesn't rebuild what doesn't exist. If there is no history, no on-chain trail and no bank statement for a period, it is documented as impossible to rebuild and the approach taken is explained, but nothing is made up.

It doesn't guarantee an outcome with the tax authorities. No methodology does, and you should be wary of anyone who promises otherwise. What it does produce is a documented, consistent position, which is what can be defended.

And it isn't investment advice. We don't tell you what to buy, what to sell or when. Our field is compliance and the defence of your tax position.

items.q: How long does the process take?
items.a: It depends on the volume and, above all, on the state of the data. A well-organised portfolio of a few thousand transactions can be done in one or two weeks; a multi-chain portfolio with hundreds of thousands of records and periods to rebuild can take considerably longer. After the ingestion phase we give you a specific timeframe, because until then any estimate would be guesswork.

items.q: Do I need to give you my private keys?
items.a: No, never. We work with CSV exports, read-only API keys and public wallet addresses. A private key isn't needed to read a transaction history, and you shouldn't give yours to anyone.

items.q: What if I already have a report made with Koinly or CoinTracking?
items.a: It works as a starting point and saves us the ingestion phase. What we do is review the reconciliation: internal transfers, the acquisition cost of anything received without a purchase, the treatment of swaps, and spam. If the report has already been filed with the AEAT, the work is different, and it's worth looking at it alongside our tax litigation page.

items.q: Do you work with any blockchain and protocol?
items.a: With most of them. Chains and protocols with public explorers and accessible data don't usually cause problems. The difficult cases are very small protocols, chains with no maintained explorer, or platforms that have already shut down, and in those cases we tell you before we start.

The reconciled portfolio is built from the very beginning of your activity, not from the tax year you want to declare: without the earlier history there is no reliable acquisition cost. If rebuilding it reveals tax years that were declared incorrectly or not declared at all, we tell you and look at the options for regularising them together.

cierre.body: Tell us roughly how many transactions you have, which exchanges and chains you use and which tax years concern you. With that, we'll tell you what work lies ahead and give you an indicative timeframe and price.
